summary: Defines OSPF-TE extensions for advertising the general network element constraints described in RFC 7579, so routers can share information about switching and label restrictions in GMPLS networks.

eli5.summary: A way for routers to tell each other about their quirks, like what they can and cannot connect.

questions: ospf extension for network element constraints
what is the ospf-te connectivity matrix sub-tlv
what is port label restrictions sub-tlv
subtitle: Two new OSPF-TE sub-TLVs let routers advertise switching and label limits in GMPLS networks.

tldr.problem: In some GMPLS-controlled technologies, such as wavelength switched optical networks, nodes and links have limits on what can connect to what and which labels can be used, and path computation needs to know them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7580 defines two OSPF-TE sub-TLVs: Connectivity Matrix (type 14) in the Node Attribute TLV and Port Label Restrictions (type 34) in the Link TLV. Their contents are encoded as defined in RFC 7579.
tldr.outcome: Routers can flood these constraints in Opaque LSAs, and the RFC gives ways to split them across LSAs so they stay under the MTU.

today: RFC 7580 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2015. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The encodings it relies on are in RFC 7579.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Some data-plane technologies that need a GMPLS control plane impose extra constraints on switching and on label assignment. Some also need non-local label assignment, for example the wavelength continuity constraint in Wavelength Switched Optical Networks (WSONs, RFC 6163). That can require link-by-link label availability during path computation and label assignment.

RFC 7579 defines protocol-neutral encodings for this information. RFC 7580 builds on it and extends OSPF to carry it, enhancing the GMPLS TE properties defined in RFC 3630, RFC 4202 and RFC 4203. The information travels in OSPF-TE Link State Advertisements (LSAs), which are opaque LSAs with area flooding scope. Each has one top-level TLV (Router Address, Link, or Node Attribute from RFC 5786) with nested sub-TLVs.

The detailed encoding is not defined here; RFC 7579 provides it.
sections.eli5: Some machines have special rules about what they can connect. Routers need to hear those rules so they do not plan impossible routes.

sections.title: Node Information: The Connectivity Matrix
sections.content:
Node switching asymmetry is described by a device type (defined in RFC 7579) and a connectivity matrix, defined here as a new sub-TLV of the Node Attribute TLV, with Type 14.

If a switching device is asymmetric, it matters which input ports and labels can be switched to which labels on a given output port. The matrix can describe potential connectivity for asymmetric switches such as ROADMs, or fixed connectivity for devices such as a multiplexer (RFC 7446). The value format is in Section 2.1 of RFC 7579. One sub-TLV holds one matrix, and the sub-TLV may appear more than once in the Node Attribute TLV.

The sub-TLV may be optional depending on the technology and control plane. In WSON networks it will usually be advertised because the switches are asymmetric. If it is absent, the switches are assumed to support symmetric switching.
sections.eli5: It is a chart of which plugs on a box can be joined to which other plugs. If there is no chart, assume any plug can join any other.

sections.title: Link Information: Port Label Restrictions
sections.content:
Common link sub-TLVs such as Link ID, Administrative Group, ISCD, Link Protection Type, SRLG and TE Metric are already defined in RFC 3630 and RFC 4203. This document adds the Port Label Restrictions sub-TLV to the Link TLV, with Type 34.

It describes which labels a node and link may or may not use on a port. In a WSON these are the wavelength restrictions that links and devices such as OXCs, ROADMs and waveband multiplexers impose. The restrictions are meant to be relatively static, and may be given for the port in general or relative to a specific connectivity matrix. The value format is in Section 2.2 of RFC 7579, and the sub-TLV may occur more than once to describe a complex port constraint.

It is not advertised when there are no restrictions on label assignment.
sections.eli5: This is a note saying which colors of light a certain plug can carry and which it cannot.

sections.title: Routing Procedures and Scalability
sections.content:
All sub-TLVs are nested in top-level TLVs inside Opaque LSAs, flooded under the rules of RFC 2328, RFC 5250, RFC 3630 and RFC 4203. To avoid needless updates, static information should be kept apart from dynamic information, each in a separate top-level TLV and a separate LSA. Because the connectivity matrix is static, the LSA with the Node Attribute TLV can be updated less often. For links, the Port Label Restrictions sub-TLV could sit in its own Link TLV and LSA. Implementations typically avoid rapid, frequent updates.

Some systems might produce LSAs larger than the IP MTU, so the RFC gives splitting techniques. The two sub-TLVs can go in different LSAs, since a Link TLV can occur at most once per LSA. A single large connectivity matrix can be decomposed into sub-matrices, each with a unique matrix identifier per RFC 7579. The RFC calls an oversize matrix highly unlikely.

Path computation assumes any-port-to-any-port reachability until a Connectivity Matrix sub-TLV arrives, then uses all those received. Early on it may find a path that does not exist, and between sub-TLVs it may miss one that does; existing GMPLS mechanisms handle both. If a new sub-TLV is malformed, the proper action is to log it and ignore just that sub-TLV in path computation, not the whole LSA.
sections.eli5: Things that rarely change are sent separately so the busy messages stay small. A huge chart can be cut into pieces. A broken note is skipped, not the whole message.

sections.title: Management and IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned Type 14 (Connectivity Matrix) in the sub-registry of sub-TLVs of the TE Node Attribute TLV (value 5), and Type 34 (Port Label Restrictions) in the sub-registry of sub-TLVs of the TE Link TLV (value 2).

On manageability, no existing management tools handle these parameters. The MIB module in RFC 6825 could be augmented to report them. The RFC notes work in the TEAS working group on a YANG module for generic TE information, and says BGP-LS could realistically be extended to carry it too. Tools that examine opaque LSAs will need updating for the new sub-TLVs.
sections.eli5: Two new labels, 14 and 34, were put in the official list so everyone uses the same numbers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document introduces no security issues beyond those in RFC 3630, RFC 4203 and RFC 5250. For general security aspects of GMPLS-controlled networks it points to RFC 5920.
sections.eli5: Nothing new to worry about beyond what the earlier documents already cover.
